contests.title: Town of Moraga, Town Council

paragraphs: When my family moved to Moraga in 2017, I found an unsafe stretch of Moraga Road where kids couldn’t walk to school safely. I worked with neighbors to advocate to get it fixed. That is how I approach this job: show up, listen, get it done.

I’ve served Moraga as a Planning Commissioner, Town Councilmember, and now as Mayor, building on two decades of experience in transportation and environmental policy at the federal, state, and local levels. I’ve put that experience to work pushing our Town government toward real transparency and straightforward answers, not spin.

My priorities are direct. Protect our hillsides, open space, and the semi-rural character that makes Moraga what it is, on our own terms. Keep our finances disciplined and explained in clear language, not buried in footnotes. And require every new development to be evaluated honestly for its real effect on traffic, safety, and our ability to get out of town in an emergency, before it’s approved, not after.

I believe in this town, and in the people who show up for it. That belief is why I do this work, and why I’m asking you to keep doing it with me. I’m asking for your continued trust, and I intend to keep earning it.

I take very seriously the Moraga Town Council’s primary role of making high-quality decisions representing all citizens of our special town. Eight years ago, I committed to following through by listening, researching and making sound decisions, and I have done so. I seek your support to continue.

My professional qualifications include a BS in Mechanical Engineering, MBA in Finance, Licensed Mechanical Engineer (retired) and Certified Project Management Professional (retired). I served for over 20 years total on the Moraga Design Review Board, Planning Commission and Hacienda Foundation Board of Directors. I am a long-term member of the Kiwanis Club of Moraga Valley. I have led each of these local organizations and have been Mayor twice.

My technical and management career with Chevron included a five-year leadership assignment building competency in quality decision making for operating units across the world. I have employed this expertise as a Council Member.

I value serving with all Town Council members. We have brought diverse views and experiences, it hasn’t been perfect, but I’m proud of our accomplishments. And I commend the many local volunteers and Town Staff who are critical to Moraga’s success.

My continuing priorities for Moraga include: Championing town safety including minimizing wildfire risks; Implementing the approved Housing Element Plan while retaining our semi-rural character; Supporting our commercial sector; Continuing to expand recreational opportunities; Maintaining and enhancing our infrastructure; And especially in this increasing costs environment, continuing to be fiscally prudent to protect our financial viability.
I kindly ask for your vote.
In 2005, after a car burned in front of our home in Oakland while police dispatch put us on hold for 45 minutes, we decided to move to Moraga.

I learned that being prepared matters – so I became a trained Lamorinda CERT member and sworn Contra Costa County Animal Response Team (CART) volunteer, deployed to multiple major California emergencies including Moraga’s 2017 Campolindo hillside fire.

For over 20 years I have served this community through volunteer leadership. Elected CAPRCBM President and Director – the California Association of Park and Recreation Commissioners and Board Members – advocating for parks, trails, recreation, and open space statewide.

Moraga Parks and Recreation Commission, including as Chairperson; Moraga Traffic Safety Advisory Committee (TSAC); Moraga Bicycle Pedestrian Master Planning Committee; Livable Moraga Road Committee; and Moraga Center Specific Plan Committee.

In 2018, I walked and GIS-mapped Moraga’s trails – existing, proposed from planning documents, and key connectivity gaps – producing three reports presented to the Parks and Recreation Commission and Town Council, documenting how trail access was lost and how much could be preserved through negotiation.

Planning our parks and sports fields must reflect community needs – preserving public access is essential to what makes Moraga home. Moraga’s history of shared field agreements – like the Camino Pablo partnership funded by Measure WW – shows what’s possible when the town and other agencies work together.

My commitment: preserve Moraga’s character, parks, open spaces, and well-maintained roads – while navigating state mandates without surrendering local control and finding common ground even when it’s hard.
Prepared to serve. Ready to listen. I am asking for your vote.

As a four-year member of Moraga’s Planning Commission and current chair, I have spent hours in the room where our town’s future is shaped, reviewing development proposals and listening to neighbors on all sides of difficult land-use decisions. This experience has taught me that responsible growth isn’t about saying yes or no; it’s about asking the right questions, protecting what makes Moraga special, and planning so growth serves the community rather than straining it.

Serving on the campaign for Measure I, I worked alongside neighbors to secure resources our town needs while making the case directly to voters. That work reinforced something I already believed: Moraga residents want a real voice in decisions that affect their streets, their schools, and their open space, and they deserve leaders who will listen first and act with transparency.
As a school parent and local volunteer, I am close to the needs of Moraga families, from classroom support to community events, and I understand how decisions are made at the council level.

If elected, I will bring this hands-on planning experience, my track record of community engagement, and a commitment to open, responsive government to the Town Council. I will work to ensure that as Moraga grows to meet our region’s housing and infrastructure needs, that growth is thoughtful, sustainable, and shaped by the voices of the people who call this town home. I am running for Town Council because I love Moraga and want to “Protect What We Love, Plan for What We Need”.

contests.title: City of Orinda, City Council

paragraphs: I have had the privilege to serve as Mayor this year and am finishing my first term on the City Council. Before that, I served 7 years on the Orinda Planning Commission (Chair 2018-2020), where I had had a seat at the table for the important work on the housing element and downtown planning.

Orinda is a special place. It’s safe for kids (raising three boys here, one now at Miramonte), has real character, and has a community that gives its time and resources to make the school, sports, and civic life some of the best anywhere. As we balance the State’s mandates on housing with our own priorities for downtown, preserving community character comes first. We have to be willing to grow, though, with thriving small businesses, more housing variety, and fresh civic spaces – doing nothing is not how we will preserve the quality of life we value.

I’m a JD/MBA (Northwestern Law and Kellogg; Stanford undergrad) and have used my legal training for a career in business to be a builder and a problem solver. With 25+ years in commercial real estate and investments, I’m experienced with zoning and land use, have managed large-scale budgets with an owner’s eye to detail, and know that feasibility matters.
Through more than a decade serving Orinda I have had a chance to hear your concerns directly, and I hope I have proven that I am a careful listener, thoughtful, and fair.
Learn more at: www.voteiverson.com.

I am honored by the opportunity to serve on the Orinda City Council and make a positive impact on our community. During my term, I have also served on the board of Recycle Smart and as a liaison to Orinda Parks & Recreation, Art in Public Places, School 2×2, Historical Society, and the Orinda Library.

My colleagues and I have faced many challenging issues, working collaboratively to identify and implement what’s best for Orinda. The City has made significant strides to address our top wildfire safety concern. We launched OrindaReady.com to centralize resources and highlight a wildfire simulation tool that estimates evacuation time. To improve emergency evacuation capacity and provide additional egress, the City constructed two median openings on Camino Pablo. To foster economic development, the City set up DowntownOrinda.com and initiated a façade improvement program. Civic beautification projects that stand out include the first-ever Welcome to Orinda monument, new median landscaping, new library plantings, and future hanging flowerpots.

Public service is essential; it’s about caring for our city and helping others. For over 40 years, I have been passionate about my hometown and its citizens as a volunteer leader in the Orinda schools, Orinda Garden Club, Girl Scouts, and Santa Maria Church. Serving on your City Council culminates my volunteer, local and legal knowledge. I serve with an open mind, respect, common sense, and compassion. With your support for my re-election, I will continue to work to help Orinda remain strong and prepared for the future.
Facts matter. Evidence should guide our decisions for a safe and vibrant Orinda.

As a physicist and the mother of an Orinda public school student, I know that without evidence, even well-intentioned decisions can have serious, unwanted consequences. I have proudly called Orinda home for more than 15 years and served as a substitute teacher in Orinda’s public schools.

I am committed to improving the safety of students who walk and bicycle to school. I will work with you to ensure our road network supports efficient daily travel and safe evacuation during emergencies. I also care deeply about protecting Orinda’s creeks and expanding access to the natural spaces that make our community unique.

As a first-time candidate, I will make City government more transparent and accessible by supporting live remote access and recordings for all public City meetings (beyond City Council). I will also create regular opportunities for you to speak with me. Please visit juanafororinda.com and share your thoughts.

I earned degrees in Physics and Mathematics from Berkeley and a Ph.D. in Physics. Throughout my career leading complex scientific and engineering teams, I have learned that the best decisions come from testing assumptions and following the facts. I believe good government should do the same.
I ask for your vote so that together we can ensure Orinda’s future is guided by facts, evidence-based decisions, and community participation.
I am an attorney and business owner. I’ve lived in Orinda for 22 years, have raised my three children in our public schools, and have pride and gratitude for all that we enjoy.
It’s been my honor to serve you on the Orinda City Council since 2022, and last year, to serve as Mayor. I promised to move Orinda forward while preserving the quality of life that we all cherish.

I’ve paid particular attention to protecting our community from wildfire. I have led Orinda to become a model city regarding evacuation and safety planning, fire prevention, community education, and regional coordination. We have accomplished much, but we are not done. I hope to continue this important work.

I’ve worked with downtown businesses to make sure the city is giving our downtown core the attention it needs to be successful by nurturing current businesses and helping to attract new ones. I’ve tackled critical infrastructure needs, maintaining excellent roads and drains, while protecting fiscal reserves. I’ve promoted upgrades like sidewalks, so our families have safer routes to school. I’ve championed improved public spaces including our new dog park, dedicated pickleball hours, upcoming playground remodel, and beautification efforts.
If you honor me with another term, I’ll continue to focus on creating an Orinda that is safe, prepared, welcoming, vibrant, and economically thriving – a place that we are all proud to call home.
I’d be honored to receive your vote. To learn more, please visit latika4orinda.com.

contests.title: City of Pinole, City Council

paragraphs: My service to the City of Pinole began in 1995 when I was hired by the Police Department as a Community Service Officer. Pinole quickly became my home. My wife and I moved to the City the following year, bought our house in 2000, and raised our two children in Old Town.

My experience includes 28 years with the Police Department. As Police Commander and Acting Chief of Police, I managed operations, support services, personnel and budgeting. I worked closely with every city department and have broad knowledge in city functions. I have extensive experience in labor representation and relations, having held several board positions, including president, with the Pinole Police Employees Association, and the Peace Officers Research Association of California Bay Area Chapter. Additionally, I have over 15 years of volunteer service with the Special Olympics Northern California (2022 Law Enforcement Volunteer of the Year), and the Pinole Hercules Little League (coach, umpire, safety officer, and vice president).

Working and living in Pinole for nearly three decades, I have watched the quality of life in our community ebb and flow, and I have had the opportunity to observe the factors contributing to both cycles. Pinole currently faces some significant challenges: understaffed Public Safety, deteriorating infrastructure, and budget shortfalls. We must make changes to our financial priorities in order to preserve the beauty and prosperity of our city, our home. I believe fiscal responsibility begins with community safety, maintenance of infrastructure, and attracting and sustaining local businesses.

As a Pinole City Council member, I will continue my commitment to representing All who call our city Home, and helping shape a Pinole that addresses current issues in a meaningful way while planning for a thriving tomorrow.

As a daughter of refugees, Christy grew up below the poverty line, yet witnessed her family practicing revolutionary love by using what little resources they had to help others. These values fuel Christy as a mother, advocate, and business owner. Christy believes we deserve more than just survival, we deserve to thrive — governance that works for the community, safe and vibrant neighborhoods, and a future where all Pinole residents have equal opportunity to the resources they need.

As Pinole Planning Commissioner with the commission’s support, Christy successfully advocated for the ad-hoc Community Engagement Committee and to add a 2nd Public Comment portion to increase equitable civic engagement.
As Contra Costa Women and Girls Commissioner, with commission’s support, Christy organized the inaugural Sheroes panel to celebrate women in our Pinole community who have made history with Herstory.
As Contra Costa Developmental Disability Commissioner, with the commission’s support, they created a School Aged Working Group to address gaps in services, programming, and support.

We all want the people we elect to authentically represent us. We must decide if we want to keep kicking the can down the road and balance the budget on the working class, or elect Christy to help Pinole progress forward as a city.
Accountability, Safety, Affordability – Progress for All cannot wait!
Learn more at www.christylamjulian.com

I am seeking appointment to the Pinole City Council because I believe our community deserves transparent and accountable leadership. Pinole is a city with great potential, and I am committed to preserving what makes it a wonderful place to live while planning responsibly for its future.

Professionally, I have built my career leading operations, improving efficiency, and solving problems. My priorities are maintaining safe neighborhoods, practicing responsible fiscal management, supporting local businesses, and ensuring City Hall remains accessible and responsive to every resident.

Before transitioning into operations, I spent several years working at a medical hospital, as an Emergency Room Unit Coordinator. Working alongside physicians, nurses, EMTs, firefighters, and law enforcement gave me a deep appreciation for the dedication, sacrifice, and professionalism of our first responders and strengthened my commitment to public service.

Alongside my professional experience, I am pursuing an Associate of Arts in Criminology to deepen my understanding of public policy, community safety, and the responsibilities of effective public leadership. I believe lifelong learning will help me better serve our community.

It would be an honor to serve the residents of Pinole. I am ready to work hard, listen carefully, and help build a stronger, safer, and more vibrant community for current and future generations. If you see me around town, please say hello. I welcome the opportunity to meet my fellow Pinole neighbors, hear your ideas and concerns, and work together to keep Pinole a community we are all proud to call home.

I am running for City Council to give back to the community where I have lived for the past twenty years. Raised in Pinole and a proud Pinole Valley High School alumni, I went on to earn a B. A. in Political Science at UC Berkeley. After college, I devoted myself to public service by pursuing a career in the California State Senate. This role allows me to advocate for my community at the state level and build relationships with local leaders across the region.

I serve on our city’s Planning Commission as the youngest chair in the city’s history. As a Commissioner, I have learned about responsible development, protecting our environment, and governance. I value what our residents care about while advocating for their needs. I worked with my colleagues on the Commission to devise concepts for the redevelopment of the Appian 80 Shopping Center. I presented to the City Council a united commission proposal that best serves and transforms this space for our community.

Pinole has made me successful, and my passion for public service has led me to want to serve as your representative. My plan for Pinole puts our city first, ensuring we make progress in paving our roads, revitalizing economic development, and maintaining effective response times for emergencies. It would be an honor to be your representative, and I humbly ask for your vote. You may learn more about me and my campaign at www.gabeforpinole.com or reach me directly at
[email removed].

I am Tina Brown, and I know what it means to be overlooked. I have slept in doorways, gone hungry, and grown up without knowledge of my lineage. At an early age I became a statistic in a system that had already determined my future.

By grace, I persevered through hardship, raised five children, and built a career in service to others. In 2023, after the loss of my husband I was emotionally and financially depleted, left with only one cent. In my deepest moments of despair, I was reminded of God’s presence and that I was not alone. My daughter and the city of Pinole welcomed me in.

I bring 32 years of public service experience, including 15 years dedicated to direct community support. My faith has taught me to lead with compassion and empathy, to listen without judgment, and to honor each person with respect.

I am running for Pinole City Council to advocate for children with special needs, parents seeking support, teachers in need of resources, seniors who deserve to age in place, families living one emergency away from homelessness, and future homeowners striving to afford a down payment.

My priorities include responsible fiscal stewardship, safe neighborhoods, thriving local businesses, expanded housing opportunities, and meaningful partnerships among schools, nonprofit organizations, faith communities, and city government.
I will trust in God and the community for guidance, I have learned the importance of listening, and stand ready to serve the City of Pinole with faith, empowerment, compassion.

contests.title: City of Pittsburg, City Council

paragraphs: As your incumbent City Councilmember, I respectfully ask for your vote to continue serving the City of Pittsburg. As a longtime resident deeply involved in our community, city development, and local government, I remain committed to building a safer, stronger, and more prosperous Pittsburg for future generations.

During my time on the City Council, I have worked to maintain fiscal responsibility through balanced budgets, attract new businesses that create local jobs, and support investments that strengthen our community. I have partnered with our Police Department, schools, nonprofits, and community organizations to enhance public safety, improve quality of life, and expand opportunities for residents. I remain committed to supporting local labor, green growth, and services for youth, seniors, and veterans.

My experience includes serving as former Chair of the Planning Commission, a union UFCW Local 5 member and shop steward for 36 years, Board Member of the Sierra Club Delta Group, current Chair of the East Contra Costa County Habitat Conservancy, Board Member of MCE, and member of the Green Empowerment Zone Governing Board.

These leadership roles have prepared me to make responsible decisions that balance economic opportunity, environmental stewardship, and sound financial management. Together, we have made meaningful progress, and I am committed to continuing Pittsburg’s positive momentum while preserving the values that make our city a wonderful place to live, work, play and raise a family.
I would be honored to earn your vote.

I’m running for Pittsburg City Council because I love this community, and I believe Pittsburg deserves a strong, independent voice someone who listens to residents, asks the hard questions, and puts Pittsburg first.

Pittsburg is my lifelong home. I was born and raised here, and my family’s roots in this community go back generations. This is more than a city I live in it’s the community that shaped me, my family, and who I am today.

I’m a full-time mother, wife and homeowner, and being a mother has made me think deeply about the future we are creating for our children. I want to help build a Pittsburg where the next generation has opportunity and a reason to be proud of where they come from.

My professional background includes banking, compliance, business consulting, startups, acquisitions, sales, logistics, and operations. As a former banking Compliance Officer and business leader, I’ve learned the importance of oversight, accountability, responsible decision-making, and asking the right questions. l’ve led teams, managed budgets, improved operations, and worked with diverse stakeholders to solve complex problems.

I’m not running because I want to be a politician. I’m running because I believe residents deserve to be heard. I will advocate for transparency, accountability, responsible growth, and meaningful resident participation.
I’m ready to serve the community that has always been home with my head high, my heart in the right place, and Pittsburg always in mind.
C.C. Cardinalli-Macaluso

Pittsburg raised me. I graduated from Pittsburg High. My grandfather started our family real estate business in 1946, my dad brought it to Pittsburg in the 1970s, and I run it today on Railroad Avenue. My wife and I are raising six kids in this town because we believe in Pittsburg.

Our city faces a five million dollar deficit, cutting the things that make Pittsburg home: Buchanan Pool, youth programs, Small World Park. A data center beside people’s homes, a school, and a church. We already lost Target, Bombardier, and the steel mill. You cannot cut your way to a thriving city. You grow your way there.

Growing Pittsburg is what I have done my whole career. As CEO of the Pittsburg Chamber of Commerce, I helped our small businesses survive COVID and reach every relief dollar available. I served on the Planning Commission, on the citizens committee overseeing your Measure P tax dollars, and on the school district bond oversight committee. I am a past president of Pittsburg Rotary.

My priorities are simple. Grow the tax base so we can fix our roads and keep our pool open without raising your taxes. Protect services for youth and seniors. Beautify the gateways to our city. Make city hall ask residents before big projects are approved, not after.
I have spent my life betting on Pittsburg. I am asking for one of your three votes.
Wolf Croskey
www.vote4wolf.org

My name is Amhari Perkins, and I am honored to be a candidate for Pittsburg City Council. I am a wife, mother, healthcare professional, and proud Pittsburg resident who believes our city deserves leadership built on transparency, accountability, and community partnership.

For more than a decade, I worked in healthcare, where I learned the value of listening, collaboration, ethical decision-making, and advocating for people when it matters most. Those experiences taught me that the strongest leaders bring people together, rely on facts, and make decisions with integrity and compassion.

Like many residents, I became more involved in local government because I saw how important community participation is in shaping Pittsburg’s future. I have worked alongside neighbors to increase civic engagement, encourage respectful dialogue, and ensure residents are informed and involved in decisions that affect our neighborhoods.

If elected, I will prioritize transparent government, responsible economic development, fiscal responsibility, public safety, environmental stewardship, and meaningful public engagement. I believe growth should strengthen our community while protecting the quality of life that makes Pittsburg a wonderful place to live, work, and raise a family.

As a mother raising my children here, I have a personal investment in the future of our city. I will always approach every decision by asking what is best for our residents today and for future generations.
I would be honored to earn your trust and your vote. Together, we can build a Pittsburg that is transparent, inclusive, financially responsible, and better for the future.

statement.designation: I’m Pauline Johnson, and I’m a wife, mother, and proud Pittsburg homeowner.
paragraphs: Our city approved a 350,000 square foot data center in 2024. Notice went to residents within 400 feet, so the school 500 feet away found out this year with the rest of us. This year, we also uncovered the budget is short five million dollars, with cuts ahead. Our library is now closed Mondays. A million dollars left this city in a phishing scam.

In June, I did something about it. The data center documents ran thousands of pages, English only. You deserve to know what’s happening in your own backyard. So I used my engineering background to build a four-language website, then took it further: flyers to thousands of homes, community meetings, council sessions.
That work became revealing: We asked for a pause, time to learn and have a real voice before moving forward.

That’s why I’m running: to give residents a vote in the room, not just a comment card. As councilmember, I’ll push for smart growth that fits our current zoning and includes Pittsburg’s union workers, data-driven decisions residents can hold us accountable to, departments showing their work quarterly, roads like Leland fixed instead of deferred, and real notice before decisions are made, not after, because the legal minimum isn’t enough.
Residents have a vision for our city’s future. It’s on the city to capture it, so we grow together.

Pittsburg has always been home. As a fifth generation Pittsburg High School family, I grew up learning that strong communities are built by neighbors who care for one another and leaders who show up, listen, and work together to solve problems.

I am honored you have chosen me to serve as your mayor and councilmember. Professionally, I have spent more than 20 years leading teams, solving complex challenges, and building partnerships that strengthen organizations and communities. Those experiences reinforced my belief that consistent leadership, thoughtful decision-making, transparency, and collaboration produce the best results for everyone.

Together, we have made Pittsburg stronger, investing $202M in roads and infrastructure, $11M in parks, and $6M in community facilities to meet our city’s growing needs. I am running for re-election because our progress is real, but the work is not finished. Pittsburg’s best days are still ahead.

I remain committed to making Pittsburg a city where it’s affordable for families to live, businesses grow, neighborhoods stay safe, and infrastructure keeps pace with growth. I continue to demand greater transparency, access to information, and community engagement on major projects and decisions.

I am honored to be endorsed by local leaders and workers, and would be honored to earn your vote so we can keep building a stronger Pittsburg together. Please contact me anytime at mailto:[email removed]. Thank you!
My name is Alvin Nelson, and I am running for Pittsburg City Council because our residents deserve transparent, accountable, and responsive leadership that puts our community first.

I am a Human Resources Professional with over 20 years of experience as a business leader, a husband, father, and proud Pittsburg resident. My career has been built on solving difficult problems, listening to people, managing resources responsibly, and holding organizations accountable. I also serve my community through volunteer leadership and neighborhood advocacy.

I do not support data centers in Pittsburg. I will advocate for an immediate moratorium on new data center applications and future approvals. I will oppose Phases 2 and 3 of the proposed data center development and support giving Pittsburg voters a direct voice before any future expansion moves forward. Major development decisions should be transparent and include meaningful public input.

My priorities also include safer neighborhoods, well maintained parks and streets, responsible spending, reliable public services, economic opportunities for residents and local businesses, and a City Hall that listens and responds to the people it serves.

Residents should never feel ignored when decisions affect their families, neighborhoods, and quality of life. You deserve leaders who ask tough questions, communicate openly, and are accountable for their decisions.
If elected, I will listen, lead with integrity, and put Pittsburg residents first.
I respectfully ask for your vote for Pittsburg City Council on November 3, 2026.

My public service began with the Navy. I used Veteran benefits to graduate from SFSU Paralegal Program and to attend Oakland College of Law. I did a Paralegal Internship at Oakland City Attorney’s Office. A Pittsburg resident for 31 years, I have served on several Boards/Commissions. First at Stoneman HUD Housing for nine years. Beginning as Chair of the Food Service program, then Vice President, then in 2024 as the first minority woman Board President. I‘m Afro-American/Native American. I’m proud of my rich and diverse heritage. My Great Grandfather was a Court Interpreter for Native Americans for Federal Judge Robert L. William’s Courtroom.

My community service is also diverse: Chair of Pittsburg Community Advisory Commission, PUSD Student Attendance Review Board, East Contra Costa NAACP, Contra Costa Racial Justice Oversight Board (Criminal Diversion), 2nd Vice Chair Pittsburg Elks Lodge #1474, Vice Chair Fifty Plus Club, Contra Costa Council on Aging (Housing Committee) and Vice Chair BART Police Civilian Review Board. My Environmental groups include: 350 Contra Costa Action (including Healthy Homes Project), 350 Bay Area, Sierra Club, and a graduate of Shoreline Academy. As a Councilmember on Metropolitan Transportation Commission/Association of Bay Area Governments, I address issues related to Land Use, Housing, Environmental Quality and Economic Development.
I have the experience and passion to strongly advocate for Youth, Seniors, the Environment, Affordable Housing, Transportation solutions, Public Safety , and Economic Growth. Your Chance To Be Heard.

Carolynne Born is a retired Communications and Public Relations professional whose achievements have generated awareness and support for grassroots ballot measures and corporate initiatives. She fosters pride among residents/employees, respect in the community, insight among the media, and support from stakeholders.

She is now a small business operator in pet care and advocacy, serving Central and East County. As a candidate for Pittsburg City Council, Carolynne seeks to improve citizen involvement in decision-making, influence and Quality of Life, especially as it relates to seniors, families, environmental impact, and community development. I would welcome expanded services for our seniors, such as meals and life-affirming activities.

I would like to see more community involvement at the beginning of any development project to ensure fully informed citizens. The proposed Data Center creates both economic opportunity and environmental challenge for our community. It stands as the crucial moment for Pittsburg citizens to band together and stand united in compromise and compassion. I hope to lead the way toward that compromise and create a Win-Win for our citizens. I look forward to meeting you all along the campaign trail.

I have lived in Contra Costa County since I was 5 years old, from Concord to Bay Point and now Pittsburg since 2006. I graduated from Concord High School, where I received the Principal’s Award and was elected President of the first Latinos Unidos Club. I helped organize the school’s first multicultural event, worked with students on conflict resolution, and organized a university field trip.

I enrolled at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo in Aeronautical Engineering and served on the Student Body Board of Directors. After major cuts in aerospace, military, and NASA programs following the fall of the Soviet Union, I changed my major to History and studied abroad in Mexico City for a year. After earning my BA in History, I taught for three years as a substitute and later as a World History teacher.

I am happily married and a father of three. Today, I own a successful business, employ local workers, and help clients protect their income, assets, and investments. I am a past President of the Contra Costa Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, current President of the Pittsburg Rotary, and Treasurer of United Latino Voices of Contra Costa County.
I will work to reduce theft, violence, graffiti, and vandalism, invest in our residents and future generations, and protect Pittsburg’s quality of life.
Stop the Pittsburg Data Center!
More info: WhiteEagle.info

contests.title: City of Pittsburg, City Clerk

paragraphs: Hi, I am Angel Rodriguez, and I am running for Pittsburg City Clerk.

I believe our City deserves a City Clerk who is transparent, accessible, and prepared to meet the needs of a growing community. The City Clerk’s office is more than an administrative function; it is how the public interacts with their local government. Every resident should have confidence that their government is open, responsive, and accountable.

I will bring a modern approach to the office by embracing technology, improving public access to information, and ensuring that every resident can easily engage with their local government.

Our City can benefit from a new generation of leadership. Fresh perspectives and new ideas are essential to keeping Pittsburg moving forward. I respect the work that has come before, and I believe it is time to build on that foundation with energy, innovation, and a commitment to greater transparency.
I believe wholeheartedly the data center should not have been such a surprise to the community.

I will be a City Clerk who listens, communicates openly, and puts the public first. Together, we can strengthen trust in our local government by making City Hall more responsive and connected to the people it serves.
I would be honored to earn your vote and the opportunity to serve the residents of Pittsburg as your next City Clerk. https://sites.google.com/view/angel4pittsburgcityclerk/home
When it comes to City Clerk, there’s only one right lane. And that’s Melaine.

I am proud to be a candidate for Pittsburg City Clerk and to offer nearly 20 years of service to the community I proudly call home. I grew up in Pittsburg, graduated from Pittsburg High School in 1994, met my husband here, and raised our three sons here. Pittsburg is not simply where I live. It is where my family, values, and commitment to public service took shape.

As a Certified Municipal Clerk (CMC), California Professional Municipal Clerk (CPMC), and the current Director of City Clerk Services for the City of Pittsburg, I know the office, understand how City Hall works, and remain focused on the people it must serve. The City Clerk safeguards public records, supports transparent elections, helps residents access government, and ensures actions are accurate and accountable. My experience in records management, legislative processes, election administration, council support, public communication, and organizational leadership prepares me to lead from day one.

I will lead with integrity, impartiality, professionalism, and respect, while making the office more accessible, responsive, and worthy of your trust. Pittsburg has given my family so much. I am ready to keep giving back, and to keep our City Clerk’s Office moving in the right direction, forward!
I have served as your elected Clerk for 20 years, and hope to continue for the next four years. Pittsburg needs a seasoned Clerk to navigate the administration of all democratic processes.

I stay current on education sessions that inform colleagues of proposed and new laws. State directives tasking the Clerk to administer are continuing every year. The constantly changing world of technology makes it imperative that the elected City Clerk stays up-to-date with new practices and innovative ideas to assist and guide the public in understanding the role of local government.

During my tenure, I served as the Election Officer in 10 election cycles, instituted paperless agendas, webcast of City Council meetings, and broadcast of meetings on the City’s website and local CCTV stations. I also guided staff to become more efficient in responding to public records requests well within the mandated 10-day response period and also effected improvements to the Council Chamber making it more user friendly for staff and residents. I believe in full transparency for all city functions.

As a Certified City Clerk and Master City Clerk, and as the compliance officer for federal, state, and local statutes, including the Political Reform Act, the Brown Act and the Public Records Act, I am well qualified to continue this responsibility.
I appreciate your vote.

paragraphs: My name is Mark Armstrong, and it has been my privilege to serve San Ramon residents since 2021.

I was initially appointed to fill a City Council vacancy and was subsequently elected Mayor by San Ramon voters in 2024. I am seeking re-election because I believe our city benefits from experienced, steady leadership that prioritizes protecting the quality of life residents value most.

Today, one of the greatest challenges facing San Ramon is balancing the State of California’s housing mandates with the need to protect the neighborhoods that residents have worked so hard to build. While we cannot ignore these mandates, we can decide where growth makes the most sense.

Residents don’t expect City Hall to control every challenge coming from Sacramento—but they do expect their local leaders to make the best possible decisions for San Ramon. That is why San Ramon has focused much of its required housing in the City Core, repurposing underutilized office buildings and helping protect established neighborhoods, parks, open space, and community character while planning responsibly for the future.

San Ramon has earned its reputation as one of California’s most desirable communities through thoughtful planning, a focus on public safety, excellent city services, beautiful parks, and engaged residents. Preserving those strengths requires ongoing attention and responsible leadership.

Today, cities across California face significant challenges. Inflation and rising costs continue to strain municipal budgets. Residents rightly expect their city government to maintain excellent services while exercising fiscal discipline and planning responsibly for the future.

These challenges cannot be solved by rhetoric or by assigning blame. They require experience, sound judgment, and a commitment to collaborate on practical solutions. I believe the best solutions come from listening carefully, respecting different viewpoints, and bringing people together to solve problems.

I support policies that strengthen public safety, preserve our parks and open spaces, support local businesses, and ensure that new development is accompanied by appropriate infrastructure and city services.

My years on the City Council and as Mayor have prepared me to lead through these complex issues and make difficult decisions. My commitment is simple: protect our neighborhoods, keep San Ramon financially strong, preserve our exceptional quality of life, and ensure that future generations enjoy the same community we are proud to call home.
I respectfully ask for your vote and the opportunity to continue serving as your Mayor.
For more information, please visit Armstrong4SanRamon.com.
Thank you for your support.

A city thrives when its leadership is proactive, compassionate, and focused on the well-being of its families. We are fortunate to live in a beautiful, vibrant city, but to protect our quality of life, we need a clear, responsible vision for the future.
I am running for Mayor to deliver that vision. My life’s mission has been defined by service, grit, and executive leadership, and I am ready to put that experience to work for you.

Driven by the values of the immigrant experience, in 2009 San Ramon became my home, and I have dedicated my career to serving this community. My background combines the drive of a former professional athlete with the strategic mindset of a business owner and non-profit director. Building ElitSwim has been my life’s work—a commitment to coaching local youth and managing sports programs that support thousands of San Ramon families. Through decades of leading organizations, balancing budgets, and solving complex challenges, I know how to set big goals, control operational costs, and actually execute a plan.
As your Mayor, I will bring an educated, balanced, and energetic approach to City Hall, focusing on the following critical items.

Securing a genuinely balanced budget. True comfort and prosperity begin with financial health. I am committed to a transparent budget process in which ongoing city costs are covered by dependable, recurring revenues. By implementing smart strategies today, we protect vital city services and prevent future shortfalls.

Building a connected community. A responsible, accountable, and transparent City Hall belongs to the residents. I will work hard for our local government to be open, approachable, and actively listen to your concerns.

Prioritizing the wellness of our children and households. Healthy minds and bodies are the foundation of a happy city. I am deeply dedicated to advocating for youth wellness and expanding access to local mental health resources.

Driving smart local economic growth. We must keep San Ramon affordable, safe, and financially sound. I will focus on supporting our small business community, maintaining our public infrastructure, and making responsible development choices that respect our neighborhoods.

I have spent my entire life preparing to lead, build, and serve. I am ready to bring a fresh perspective, strong executive experience, and a deep passion for public service to City Hall. Let’s work together to ensure San Ramon remains a safe, healthy, and thriving place.
Thank you for your time, trust, and support.

paragraphs: In 2024, Chirag Kathrani ran for Mayor of San Ramon because the election was initially going unchallenged. Although Chirag lost to a sitting councilmember who became mayor, the experience strengthened his commitment to public service and showed him how often community voices go unheard.

Since that election, Chirag has dedicated significant time to engaging residents and helping them participate in local government. Chirag founded the Open Governance Initiative to amplify community voices and make government decisions easier to understand. That initiative has since grown into OpGov.News, a local news organization where communities are covered by journalists who live in and understand those communities.

Through OpGov.News, Chirag and his team do more than report what happens at City Council and school board meetings. They ask questions on behalf of residents, follow up on concerns raised during public comment, and hold public officials accountable. OpGov.News now publishes hyperlocal news throughout the Tri-Valley and delivers a physical newspaper directly to residents.

Chirag believes democracy is strongest when elections are competitive and residents have meaningful choices. After analyzing previous election results, Chirag found that voter participation often declines when candidates run without opposition. That is why he has worked to engage young people, encourage community members to consider public service, and help prospective candidates understand how to run for office.
Chirag believes meaningful change can happen only when elected representatives are accessible, responsive, and genuinely willing to listen.

One clear example is San Ramon’s appeal process. In neighboring cities, the starting fee to appeal a planning decision is generally around $300. San Ramon, however, requires residents to pay an initial deposit of $2,500, and the final cost can become a financial burden. Residents should not have to spend a fortune simply to ask their elected representatives to review a government decision. Chirag will work to establish reasonable appeal fees, clear timelines, and meaningful access to the City Council.
Chirag welcomes criticism because honest criticism helps public officials learn, improve, and remain accountable. He will listen respectfully, including when there is disagreement.
Chirag is running to represent you—and only you—not political establishments or special interests.

It’s critical that we work regionally on significant transformative issues like housing and transportation. I’m energized to continue our city’s role in that work.
I am proud to have earned wide bipartisan support, including endorsements from local, regional, and state elected officials, as well as business leaders and labor groups.
I humbly ask for your vote. Let’s continue to build our safe, healthy, and vibrant community together.

I am running for City Council because I believe Walnut Creek can move forward without losing what makes it special. Our city will benefit from a fresh perspective, but it also needs a steady hand: someone who will put practical solutions and residents’ needs ahead of politics.

I will work to reduce traffic, make our streets safer, keep our neighborhoods secure, protect parks and open spaces, support local businesses and our arts community, and plan thoughtfully for housing and growth. Residents deserve a City Council that is accessible, transparent, financially responsible, and focused on results.

As a Planning Commissioner and former Parks, Recreation and Open Space Commissioner, I understand how much local decisions affect people’s everyday lives. My experience has taught me that strong local leadership starts with listening, asking the right questions, and finding common ground.

I am proud to have earned support from residents across Walnut Creek, from young families and small business owners to seniors and longtime community leaders. I will always make decisions independently and put our community first.
As a parent of young children, I think about the kind of city we are building for the next generation. I want our children to inherit a community that is safe, welcoming, and prepared for the future.
I would be honored to earn your vote.

paragraphs: The Lamorinda area has been my home since my children were small, and I love it. The safety and wellbeing of the community is of prime importance to me.
In recent years I have become increasingly aware of the fire danger in this area. As my awareness of potential fire danger grew, I came to appreciate the role of the MOFD.

MOFD was formed in 1997 by the residents of Moraga and Orinda. Its defined purpose was to use property taxes for fire protection. These taxes were allocated for fire protection by Prop 13, to be used by the communities which generated these taxes.
The voters’ pamphlets for this election are still available (see www.Steve4MOFD.info/MOFD-voter-pamphlets)
As a Director of our MOFD, I will uphold the original intent in its formation.
I have worked hard to learn about the inner workings of the district.
I want safe communities for all of us, and am willing to work very hard on behalf of this commitment.
Neighbors,

I am asking your support to become your Moraga Orinda Fire District Board member, representing Division 3. MOFD’s continued success is vital to protecting the health and well-being of our community. Its current strong position is a tribute to years of hard work in the District and our broader community. Maintaining this high level of readiness requires a continuous commitment of time, money and effort, an investment in our community’s safety that cannot be neglected. Success depends on MOFD and our community working together in a collaborative and cost-effective manner. As a Board Member I will work to support MOFD’s engagement in these key areas.

I am Past President and current Treasurer of the Rotary Club of Orinda and also have been Assistant Governor for the 5 Rotary Clubs in our area. After completing a PhD in Immunology, I worked in discovery and development of vaccines for Merck, Chiron and Novartis. Later I joined the nonprofit PATH where I directed a program to assist developing country vaccine manufacturers. Finally I served as President of the nonprofit Global Healing, which works to improve the quality of pediatric care in low-income countries.

My final assignment before retiring was as Deputy Commanding General, 3rd Medical Deployable Support Command, Ft. Gillem, GA. Providing emergency medical transportation is a large part of MOFD’s mission and also a vital element of Army Medicine. My duties included leadership of Army medical units, including evacuation assets, at various levels of command. I believe this experience will be useful to MOFD. This military information does not imply endorsement by the Department Of War or the Department Of The Army.
I will very much appreciate your support in the coming election.

paragraphs: Technology is advancing fast, and that’s good news for our fire district. New tools are making fire prevention, response, and recovery smarter and more effective every year. I want to help the Moraga-Orinda Fire Protection District put those tools to work for our community.

For more than 40 years, I’ve worked in the geospatial industry, building technology that supports firefighters and first responders. I spent 28 years as an executive at ESRI, the world’s leading Geographic Information Systems (GIS) company. That experience taught me how to identify practical solutions, learn from proven approaches, and bring the right experts to the table. I’ll use that knowledge to strengthen how our District protects the nearly 38,500 residents across our 42 square miles.

Our District faces real challenges. We include areas designated as Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zones, and our crews respond to more than 3,000 incidents each year. Smart planning and modern tools can help our firefighters work faster, safer, and more efficiently. I believe I can help make that happen.

I also understand the power of community. As a former board member of the Southern California Mountains Foundation, I saw firsthand how local organizations and engaged citizens can expand what our firefighters are able to do. Strong partnerships and open communication make our whole District safer.

I hold a degree in geography from UCLA and a Master’s from the University of Redlands. I moved to the LaMorinda area in 2015 and quickly found my home here. I love our access to nature, our small-town charm, and our easy connection to San Francisco. Protecting this special place is personal for me.

I’m asking for your vote so I can bring my technical expertise, board experience, and deep commitment to our community to the MOFD Board of Directors. Together, we can keep Moraga, Orinda, Canyon, and Bollinger Canyon safe for years to come.
As an Orinda resident and your Division 4 director on the Moraga-Orinda Fire District board, I ask for your support to continue the work we have started together.

We live in one of the most beautiful — and most fire-vulnerable — regions in California. The hills above us are not an abstract risk; they are our neighborhoods and our homes. As a director and Firewise Ambassador, I have worked to put science and technology to work for our safety: hands-on home-hardening assessments, and expanded defensible-space education so homes are prepared before the next Diablo wind event — not after. I also publish free, step-by-step ember-protection guides on roemerwise.com. This work is never finished, and I am committed to continuing it.

We expanded ambulance service with an innovative single role paramedic program that increased service availability while reducing the pressure on district pension obligations. We acquired a new administration building, paying cash with no interest expenses, for essential staff offices.

Fiscal stewardship is essential. MOFD is a public trust, and every dollar the district spends belongs to the taxpayers of Moraga and Orinda. I worked to bring discipline and transparency to our budgeting, and I am a consistent voice for addressing long-term pension obligations honestly — not deferring hard decisions to future boards and residents. We invested tax revenue in safe Treasury bills that increase our returns, and hired new investment advisors to manage investments to protect post employment benefits for our firefighters. Sound finances are what make good service, to our firefighters and to our community, sustainable.

I believe in a board that works. Special district governance at its best is quiet, competent, and collaborative. Directors aligned on mission — even when they disagree on specifics — accomplish far more than those focused on conflict. contests.title: Regional Transit Measure
contests.question: To prevent major service cuts to BART and other transit, avoid increased traffic, and reduce pollution by: Preserving BART, Caltrain, VTA, SamTrans, AC Transit, Muni, other transit for everyone, including workers, students, seniors, persons with disabilities; Supporting transit safety, cleanliness, affordability, reliability; Repairing targeted roads/potholes; Requiring financial transparency, oversight, accountability; shall the measure enacting a 0.5% (Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara counties), and 1% (San Francisco) sales tax for 14 years generating approximately $980,000,000 annually, be adopted?
contests.threshold: 50%+1 of all votes cast in the five Bay Area counties
contests.proposal: This measure was placed on the ballot by voter initiative, signed by the requisite number of voters within the Public Transit Revenue Measure District (“District”). The District was created by the Legislature through Senate Bill 63 (“SB 63”) in 2025 (Government Code sections 67700-67788), which was enacted to preserve and improve public transit service in the San Francisco Bay Area. The District comprises the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara, and the City and County of San Francisco, and is governed by the same board that governs the Metropolitan Transportation Commission (“MTC”). SB 63 authorizes District voters to approve a retail transactions and use tax (commonly referred to as a sales tax) for specified purposes. This measure would impose a tax of 0.5% in the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara and 1.0% in the City and County of San Francisco. The tax would be imposed and collected in largely the same manner as a state-imposed sales tax. The tax would be in effect for 14 years and would not count toward the statutory limit on combined local sales tax rates. It is estimated that the tax would raise approximately $980 million per year. After payment of defined costs, including election costs and administrative expenses, the District must transfer all remaining revenues to MTC and county transportation agencies for distribution and expenditure according to percentages set forth in the measure, which vary by county and recipient. Recipients include BART, Muni, Caltrain, AC Transit, Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority, San Francisco Bay Ferry, Golden Gate Transit, smaller bus operators in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, and county transportation agencies. Revenues would also support free and reduced-cost transit transfers, expansion of the Clipper START reduced-fare program, accessibility programs, mapping and wayfinding and transit priority projects and programs, and repavement projects for roads served by fixed-route transit. While the tax would be imposed throughout the District, the allocation of revenue generated in each county, and the authorized uses of those funds, would vary. For example, 64.70% of all revenues generated in Alameda County would be allocated to BART for transit operations expenses. By contrast, 84.37% of all revenues generated in Santa Clara County would be allocated to the Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority for public transit expenses and roadway repavement projects on roads served by fixed-route transit. Such repavement projects would be an authorized use of measure revenues in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties, but would not be authorized in the City and County of San Francisco. Revenue allocation is set forth in Section 12 of the measure. Tax revenues would be subject to accountability requirements in SB 63, which requires BART, Muni, AC Transit, and Caltrain to undergo financial efficiency reviews and adopt implementation plans and authorizes MTC to withhold funds from any of those operators for noncompliance. The measure would also require an independent oversight committee to review whether all revenues are distributed as required. The tax would become effective if approved by a majority of those voting on the measure throughout the entire District.

contests.question: Shall the measure supporting high-quality education in local high schools by:
contests.summary:
The governing board of the Acalanes Union High School District has adopted a resolution proposing a parcel tax (a qualified special tax).

If this measure passes, beginning on July 1, 2027, the current parcel tax would be increased by $168 annually on parcels of taxable real property within the District for eight years, expiring on June 30, 2035. Based on information from the County Auditor-Controller’s Office, there are two existing parcel taxes totaling $301 per parcel annually. If this measure passes, the total amount of annual parcel taxes would be $469 per parcel.

The parcel tax would apply to each parcel of taxable real property in the District. A parcel of taxable real property is any unit of real property in the District that receives a separate tax bill for property taxes from the Contra Costa County Treasurer-Tax Collector’s Office.

The ballot measure includes certain exemptions. Upon proper application to the District, the District may exempt any parcel from the parcel tax that is owned and occupied as a principal residence by (1) a person 65 years of age or older; (2) a person receiving Supplemental Security Income for a disability; or (3) a person receiving Social Security Disability Insurance benefits, whose yearly income does not exceed 250 percent of the 2012 federal poverty guidelines issued by the United States Department of Health and Human Services. Additionally, property that is otherwise exempt from property taxes shall also be exempt from the parcel tax.

The ballot measure states that the proceeds of the parcel tax will be used to support “high-quality education in local high schools by attracting/retaining highly qualified teachers; continuing advanced academic programs in science, technology, engineering, math and arts that prepare students for success in college and careers; [and] maintaining manageable class sizes.” Proceeds from the parcel tax may be used only for the specific purposes set forth in the ballot measure and according to constitutional and statutory provisions.

State law requires the District’s chief fiscal officer to file an annual report with the District’s governing board that states the amount of funds received and expended in each year and the status of any projects required or authorized to be funded from the parcel tax proceeds. State law also requires the proceeds from the parcel tax to be deposited into a separate designated account. The measure also would require the District to have an appointed citizens’ oversight committee to oversee the use of parcel tax proceeds.

Of those voting on the measure, two-thirds must approve the measure for it to pass.

A ”yes” vote is in favor of authorizing the parcel tax for an eight-year period.

A “no” vote is against authorizing the parcel tax for an eight-year period.

contests.question: In order to repair and improve aging classrooms, fix deteriorating roofs, plumbing, heating, ventilation and electrical systems, remove asbestos/ lead pipes, upgrade science labs, libraries, technology and other facilities to support college/ career readiness in math, science, health, engineering, arts and skilled trades; shall Liberty Union High School District’s measure be adopted authorizing $165,000,000 in bonds at legal rates, levying $20 per $100,000 assessed value (raising $11,300,000 annually) while bonds are outstanding and all funds benefiting local schools?
contests.summary:
The California Constitution provides that school districts may issue bonds for the construction, reconstruction, rehabilitation or replacement of school facilities, including the furnishing and equipping of school facilities or the acquisition or lease of real property for school facilities, with the approval of 55% of the voters voting at an election for that purpose.

By resolution, the Liberty Union High School District has proposed that bonds of the District be issued in an amount up to $165,000,000. The measure provides that proceeds from the sale of the bonds will be used to “repair and improve aging classrooms, fix deteriorating roofs, plumbing, heating, ventilation, and electrical systems, remove asbestos/lead pipes, upgrade science labs, libraries, technology and other facilities to support college/career readiness in math, science, health, engineering, arts and skilled trades.” The specific projects are set forth in the bond project list within the measure. The measure provides that a citizens’ oversight committee will be established to ensure that bond proceeds are properly expended and that annual performance and financial audits will be conducted. The measure further provides that bond proceeds will only be used for the purposes specified in the measure and not for any other purpose.

Approval of this measure authorizes levy upon taxable property in the district to repay the bonded indebtedness, both principal and interest, in each year that the bonds are outstanding. The Liberty Union High School District has prepared a Tax Rate Statement, which represents the District’s best estimates of the property tax rates required to service the bonds. The estimated highest annual tax rate required to be levied to fund the bonds is expected to be $20 per $100,000 of assessed valuation.

Approval of the measure does not guarantee that the proposed project or projects in the District that are the subject of the bonds under the measure will be funded beyond the local revenues generated by the measure. The proposed project or projects may assume receipt of matching state funds, which could be subject to appropriation by the Legislature or approval of a statewide bond measure.

Of those voting on the measure, 55% must approve the measure for it to pass.

A ”yes” vote is in favor of authorizing the bonded indebtedness.

A “no” vote is against authorizing the bonded indebtedness.

official_args.against:
Vote No on Measure X because now is not the time to worsen East Contra Costa affordability.

Measure X increases costs for residents by $350 million of total debt service through 2058. Liberty Union High School District (LUHSD) is still paying off existing construction/maintenance bonds of Measure U (2016, $122 million, payoff 2047) and Measure A (2001, $65.4 million, payoff 2030).

A $700,000 assessed value home now pays $178.50 annually for these two bonds. Measure X’s payoff, adding another $140.00 assessment, makes the total $318.50.

LUHSD enrollment is flat, just 0.34% higher than 2016’s. So new bond funds would be used for maintenance and nice-to-have enhancements, not increased instructional capacity.

Vote No on Measure X because the expenditures are unaccountable.

In 2016 voters approved Measure U , borrowing $122 million (plus interest) to include maintenance issues similar to those cited now. Measure U was supposed to fix deteriorating roofs, plumbing, HVAC, electrical wiring, etc. Yet Measure X repeats those fixes now.

Measure X’s project list is a catch-all, not a plan. “Repair and improve aging classrooms,” “upgrade… other facilities,” and college/career readiness “in math, science, health, engineering, arts and skilled trades” covers virtually any expenditure. Voters are being asked to approve $165 million (plus $185 million interest) without a prioritized project list.

Measure X’s cited costs are “based upon projections and estimates only… and are not binding upon the District.” If home values drop, bond-payback tax rates could increase.

Vote No because Measure X’s project list isn’t sufficiently specific.

California’s Constitution requires “A list of the specific school facilities projects to be funded….” Measure X ‘s Bond Project List states “The items presented on the following list provide are (sic) the types of projects authorized…. Examples included… are not intended to limit the broader types of projects described and authorized by this measure.” Sorry, that’s not specific.

contests.question: Shall the measure supporting local quality education in West Contra Costa Unified School District, protecting core academics, science, music, arts, and career technical programs that prepare students for the changing economy; attracting and retaining qualified teachers; and maintaining mental health services and counselors to support student success; by renewing the parcel tax at the existing rate of 7.2¢/building square foot, raising approximately $10,238,737 annually for nine years, with senior exemptions, independent citizen oversight, audits, and local control, be adopted?
contests.summary:
The governing board of the West Contra Costa Unified School District has adopted a resolution proposing to extend its current parcel tax (a qualified special tax). This ballot measure asks voters to decide whether an existing parcel tax should continue to be imposed on parcels of taxable real property within the District for nine years, beginning July 1, 2027 and expiring on June 30, 2036.

If the measure passes, the tax would apply to each “improved parcel” of taxable real property in the District. An improved parcel, property with a building on it, would be taxed at a rate of 7.2 cents per square foot of total building area on the parcel. For example, the annual tax on a parcel with a 2,000 square-foot building would be $144.

Based on information from the County Auditor-Controller’s Office, the current parcel tax applying the same rate of 7.2 cents per square foot of total building area per parcel is set to expire on June 30, 2027.

The ballot measure includes certain exemptions. Upon proper application to the District, the District may exempt any parcel from the parcel tax that is owned and occupied as a principal residence by (1) a person 65 years of age or older; (2) a person receiving Supplemental Security Income for a disability; or (3) a person receiving Social Security Disability Insurance benefits, whose yearly income does not exceed 250 percent of the 2012 federal poverty guidelines issued by the United States Department of Health and Human Services.

The ballot measure states that the proceeds of the parcel tax will be used for “protecting core academics, science, music, arts and career technical programs that prepare students for the changing economy; attracting and retaining qualified teachers; and maintaining mental health services and counselors to support student success.” Proceeds from the parcel tax may be used only for the specific purposes set forth in the ballot measure and according to constitutional and statutory provisions.

State law requires the District’s chief fiscal officer to file an annual report with the District’s Board of Education that states the amounts of funds collected and expended in each year and the status of any projects required or authorized to be funded from the parcel tax proceeds. The proceeds from the parcel tax will be deposited into a District account that will be kept separate from other District accounts. Parcel tax funds will be subject to an annual financial audit. The measure also requires the District to have an independent oversight committee to oversee the use of parcel tax proceeds.

Of those voting on the measure, two-thirds must approve the measure for it to pass.

A “yes” vote is in favor of authorizing the parcel tax for a nine-year period.

A “no” vote is against authorizing the parcel tax for a nine-year period.

official_args.against:

● Measure V would now extend a parcel tax first imposed in 2004 to 2036, having annually taken $10 Million extra for 32 years by then, and guaranteeing the district an extra $10 million every year, no matter how much lower WCCUSD enrollments drop.

Consider what WCCUSD residents already pay:

● The highest school-bond tax in Contra Costa County, about $254 per $100,000 of assessed value (stacked from bonds passed in 2000, 2002, 2005, 2010, 2012, and 2020), and 3½ times Mt. Diablo Unified’s $72.

● A West Contra Costa Healthcare District parcel tax of $52 per home (higher for other properties), still collected years after Doctors Medical Center closed in 2015.

Now consider the district’s direction:

● Spending has climbed to $520 million in 2026-27 from $377 million in COVID Year 2019-20 (a 38% increase), even as enrollment has fallen 13.5 percent over those years, from 28,247 students then to 24,423 now.

A “No” vote on Measure V takes not a dollar from other record funding the schools already receive. Voting “No” requires a district already running a surplus to live within its means.

Enough is enough. Vote No on V.
